newsitem.title: USA: New York tenants rally to keep rents from rising.
newsitem.headline: New York tenants rally to keep rents from rising.

text.p: Thousands rallied Tuesday at New York's state capitol, protesting threatened changes in rent control laws in New York City.
A key Republican leader in the state Senate has threatened to let the rent laws, which for decades have governed how much millions of tenants pay, expire on June 15.
Based on vacancy rates, the laws limit how much landlords can charge for some 1.2 million apartments. Unpopular with many landlords, the laws affect 2.7 million tenants.
Many tenants worry that decontrol will lead to spiraling rent hikes and displace city residents.

The issue so inflames the passions of New Yorkers that state Senate Majority leader Joseph Bruno, who has led the drive against the laws, has blamed tenant leaders for two arson fires at his office and death threats against him.

On Tuesday, more than 8,000 people gathered outside the state Capitol building in Albany to voice their opposition to the proposed changes and to a compromise suggested by Republican Gov. George Pataki.

Wearing pink-and-white caps with the slogan "I'm a Tenant and I Vote," the protesters arrived in about 160 buses for the day-long protest. With bullhorns, they chanted "The tenants united will never be evicted."
Last week, the governor unveiled a plan called vacancy decontrol to keep the laws intact for current residents but permit market-rate rents once a tenant moves or dies.
"Vacancy decontrol is a disaster and will put enormous pressure for landlords to harass us," said Arlene Geiger, a tenant in Manhattan. "There can't be a compromise."
Some tenants, complaining that rural upstate New Yorkers ignore the plight of downstate New York City residents, proposed a boycott of upstate produce and cheese.
The boycott would be called "No Justice, No Cheese," they said.
Pataki, who spoke informally with tenant advocates and reporters before the protest, defended his plan.

"I'm very disappointed that people have used this for political reasons to frighten people as opposed to try to come up with a practical solution," he said. "The plan that I have outlined is a fair and practical solution. Literally 99 percent of the tenants who presently have rent protection in New York City will continue to have it under my plan."

Democratic Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver of New York City claimed Pataki paid more attention to the interests of 25,000 landlords and campaign contributors than to the millions who depend on the rent laws.
The battle over rent control has held up adoption of the state budget, which was due on April 1.
